meaning.evidence: The original is kept almost word for word, so nothing is lost: "It is but the work of a moment, to bound out of bed and listen at the door."

sense.evidence: The two swaps fit: "At what time is brekkie?" and "Oh, righto!" for "Oh, very well!"

authenticity.evidence: What little Aussie there is clashes with the untouched period US English around it: "At what time is brekkie?" puts slang inside a stiff construction, and "perfectly bully" is left in.

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: only "brekkie" and "Oh, righto!" change. Well short of level 2.

tone.evidence: The original's dry, genteel comedy is untouched: "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast."

flow.evidence: Reads as the original, except the jarring "At what time is brekkie?"

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original: "Some people _are_ like that."

problems.why: Slang dropped into a stiff formal question; the clash reads oddly.

A.summary: Essentially the original with two swaps; faithful but well under the brief.

meaning.evidence: All the beats are there, but it adds a frame and facts: "Back in the day, a weekend at someone's place came with its own little traps", "You check.", "up to no good by the look of 'em", and turns "We'll read it" into "You'll read the thing just out of spite".

sense.evidence: Terms fit their contexts: "have a squiz out", "Scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges", "plonk yourself down".

authenticity.evidence: Some natural lines ("Getting back to sleep? Not a hope."), but stock similes are bolted on: "like a magpie listening for a worm", "sure as eggs", "careful as a cat", "Strewth.", "Mate, that's when".

register.evidence: Heavier than level 2: "no dramas", "Mate,", "sure as eggs", "Strewth.", "beaut of a sentiment", "'em" throughout. Closer to a level 3-4 yarn. No swearing.

tone.evidence: The original's dry, mock-solemn wit becomes matey banter: "Mate, that's when you're in for a frightful mix-up." and "Lovely sentiment, beaut of a sentiment". The comedy survives but changes flavour.

flow.evidence: Lively, but with pile-ups: "Lovely sentiment, beaut of a sentiment" and "Ten past nine. That's all! Strewth."

variety.evidence: Wide and varied: "squiz", "plonk", "mob", "dodgy", "no dramas", "righto", "Strewth", "sure as eggs".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the piece, but the opening frame "Back in the day" and the asides move it towards a yarn about the piece rather than the piece.

problems.quote: Back in the day, a weekend at someone's place came with its own little traps, and getting up in the morning was the first of 'em.
problems.original: Take, for example, the matter of arising in the morning.
problems.why: Invents a framing that recasts the essay as reminiscence.

problems.quote: head cocked to one side like a magpie listening for a worm
problems.original: with head cocked on one side

problems.quote: Lovely sentiment, beaut of a sentiment
problems.original: The sentiment in this attitude is perfectly bully
problems.why: Stacked repetition; 'beaut of a sentiment' is forced.

problems.quote: Mate, that's when you're in for a frightful mix-up.
problems.original: But if you are the only guest there is apt to be a frightful misunderstanding.
problems.why: 'Mate' and the matey address push the register well past level 2 and change the tone.

B.summary: Lively and varied, but overdone for the brief, with stock similes and an invented frame.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives: "Ten past nine, that's all!", "The bath's out, too noisy." "Takes you about two seconds" renders "the work of a moment" fairly.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "have a squiz out", "Pretty scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges", "Oh, righto!". "his uni musical club" is a fair Australian equivalent.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian speech: "No chance of any more sleep now.", "Reckoned that'd be over your head, did they?", "Fair enough, I s'pose."

register.evidence: A light touch, about right for level 2: "no worries, cos", "brekkie", "squiz", "mob", "righto". No swearing.

tone.evidence: The comedy is kept, though some of its mock-formal polish goes: "It's a lovely thought, and all" for "perfectly bully", "dead careful, almost sneaky about it" for "very cautiously, almost clandestinely".

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly aloud: "Back to the door for another listen. Tick-tock-tick-tock."

variety.evidence: Varied, though "brekkie" is used twice ("What time's brekkie?", "before brekkie").

essence.evidence: Clearly the essay, slightly flattened where the arch phrasing goes: "almost sneaky about it".

problems.quote: dead careful, almost sneaky about it
Never touch a sonnet before brekkie.
problems.original: Never touch a sonnet before breakfast.
problems.why: Repeats 'brekkie'; the arch maxim reads better plain.

C.summary: Natural, light and faithful; loses a little of the original's arch formality.

meaning.evidence: Every point is kept: "It's the work of a moment to leap out of bed and listen at the door." "Scratch the bath as too noisy."

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "dodgy-looking barges", "scruffy-looking mob", "Oh, righto!". "perfectly bonzer" carries "bully" in sense.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural, but "The feeling behind it is perfectly bonzer" is a forced collocation of a dated word, and "Scratch the bath as too noisy" is a calque of the original's construction.

register.evidence: A light touch, a shade under level 2: "bonzer", "righto", "dodgy", "mob", "reckoned"; it keeps "breakfast" throughout.

tone.evidence: The genteel comic voice comes through: "Some people _are_ like that.", "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast."

flow.evidence: Smooth mostly; "Scratch the bath as too noisy." is stiff.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original, lightly retold: "How d'e do, Lorna?"

D.summary: Faithful and natural, a little light, with one forced word.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives: "Ten past nine, that's all!", "Scratch the bath, too noisy."

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "have a squiz out", "dodgy-looking barges", "Oh, righto!", "So they reckoned".

authenticity.evidence: Natural on the whole ("Odds are, if you ran your bath, you'd wake the whole house."), but "The sentiment behind it is perfectly beaut" is an odd collocation.

tone.evidence: Keeps the comic, mock-anxious voice: "Some people _are_ like that.", "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "Back to the door for another listen. Tick-tock-tick-tock."
